out: Use identification methods including scanning and CSPM.
plain: Vulnerability management is like regular building maintenance. You inspect, decide what is urgent, fix it, check the fix and keep records.
tech: Identification methods include scanning with vulnerability tools; Internet Protocol Address Management (IPAM), which tracks address use and can reveal unknown hosts; cloud security posture management (CSPM), which finds cloud misconfigurations; and source code review. Credentialed scans sign in for more accurate results, and non-credentialed scans show what an outsider would see.

Prioritization uses severity assessment plus context, and penetration test report review, which shows what was actually exploitable. Remediation may mean patching, changing configuration, applying a compensating control or formally accepting the risk. Verification confirms the fix, usually by rescanning.

Reporting can be internal, to management and asset owners, or external. External routes include a bounty program, which pays researchers for valid findings, and responsible disclosure policies, which tell researchers how to report safely. A false positive is a reported problem that does not exist. A false negative is a real problem that was missed.
terms: Internet Protocol Address Management: tracks address allocation.
Cloud security posture management: finds cloud misconfigurations.
Rating how serious a finding is.
Studying test results to understand real exploitability.
Paying researchers for valid vulnerability reports.
Rules for how researchers should report flaws.
An alert about something that is not actually a problem.
A real problem that was not detected.
eg: CSPM reports a storage bucket that became publicly readable last night, and it is closed before any data is taken.

out: Explain the roles of SIEM and related tools.
Compare NetFlow, SNMP, syslog and SCAP.
plain: Monitoring is like a building's security desk. Cameras, door sensors and alarms all feed one room. A SIEM is that room. Alert tuning makes sure the alarm does not go off each time someone opens a window.
tech: Monitoring covers systems, applications and infrastructure. Activities include log aggregation (collecting logs in one place), alerting, scanning, archiving (retaining data for later), reporting and alert tuning (adjusting rules to reduce false positives).

Tools include benchmarks, which define secure configuration targets; agents, installed on a device, and agentless collection, which reads remotely; security information and event management (SIEM), which aggregates and correlates events; antivirus; DLP; vulnerability scanners; orchestration; and a packet analyzer such as Wireshark, which examines traffic in detail. Security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) acts on alerts through playbooks. A SIEM finds and correlates, while SOAR takes the resulting actions.

Protocols: NetFlow records metadata about traffic flows but not content. Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) monitors and manages devices. syslog is a standard for sending log messages. Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) standardizes how vulnerability and configuration information is expressed, so tools can share it. Port mirroring copies traffic to a monitoring port. Dashboards summarize status. Automated alerts notify staff without someone watching. Network management systems monitor device health.

Network and supporting technology being monitored.

out: Manage accounts from provisioning through deprovisioning.
Clearly distinguish SAML, LDAP, OAuth and OpenID Connect.
plain: Federation is like using your passport in another country: a government you trust vouches for you. Single sign-on is a wristband at a festival: show it once and you can enter each stage.
OAuth is a hotel key card: it says what doors you can open, not who you are. OpenID Connect adds a photo ID on top: it tells the application who you are.
tech: Provisioning creates accounts and grants access. Deprovisioning removes them, and should happen promptly when someone leaves. Permissions assignments have implications: granting a permission to a group affects everyone in it. Identity proofing verifies a person is who they claim to be before issuing credentials. Federation allows trust between organizations, so that a person can use one identity across them.

Single sign-on (SSO) lets a user authenticate once for many applications. Security Assertions Markup Language (SAML) exchanges XML assertions between an identity provider and a service provider, and is common in enterprise SSO. Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) queries and manages directory information such as users and groups. Open Authorization (OAuth) is an authorization framework: it grants an application limited access to resources on a user's behalf using access tokens. OAuth by itself does not tell an application who the user is.

OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer built on OAuth 2.0. It adds an ID token, a signed statement about who authenticated. Use OIDC to sign users in, and OAuth to grant access to an API. OIDC does not appear in the current exam list by name, but it is essential to understanding OAuth correctly.

Account types include user accounts; privileged accounts, either global (rights across an environment) or local (rights on one system); service accounts for applications; third-party accounts for outside organizations; and emergency access accounts, sometimes called break-glass accounts, which are tightly controlled, used only in emergencies and closely monitored.
terms: Creating accounts and removing them promptly.
Granting access and understanding what it affects.
Verifying someone is who they claim to be.
Single sign-on: authenticate once for many applications.

An identity layer on OAuth 2.0 that provides an ID token.
A credential that an application uses to reach a resource.
A signed statement about who authenticated.
A standard account for a person.
An account for an application or process.

eg: Sign in with Google uses OIDC to tell a site who you are. Letting an app read your calendar uses OAuth access to an API.

out: Choose MFA factors and understand their strengths.
plain: Role-based access is like staff uniforms: nurses get nurse access. Discretionary access is like owning your diary: you decide who reads it. Mandatory access is like a military clearance, which the owner cannot change. Just-in-time access is a key checked out for one hour.
tech: In role-based access control, users are assigned roles, roles hold permissions, and a person's access is the combination of their roles. With role inheritance, a senior role automatically receives the permissions of a junior role, so an administrator role can include everything an editor can do. Least privilege means giving each role only what the job needs. Access enforcement must happen on the server for every request: hiding a button changes what users see, not what they can do.

Access control models include role-based (permissions follow job roles), rule-based (conditions apply, such as firewall rules), mandatory (the system enforces labels and clearances), discretionary (owners decide), time-based (access is limited to certain hours) and just-in-time (elevated access is granted temporarily when needed). Attribute-based access control (ABAC), which decides using attributes of the user, resource and context, is not in the current list but is common. Privileged access management (PAM) tools secure and broker admin access.

Access management includes authentication, and policies that are logical/technical (enforced by systems) or administrative/business (rules set by the organization). An access review periodically confirms that people still need their permissions.

Multifactor authentication uses different factor types. A hard token is a physical device. A soft token is an app. Biometrics measure a body feature. A one-time password (OTP) is valid once or for a short time. A backup code is a pre-generated recovery code. Phishing-resistant options such as FIDO2 security keys and passkeys are stronger than SMS or push prompts.

Password concepts: a passkey is a FIDO credential based on public key cryptography, bound to the real site, so it resists phishing. Passwordless authentication replaces passwords with such methods. Password managers generate and store unique passwords. NIST SP 800-63B-4 says that passwords used alone must be at least 15 characters, and that verifiers should check against lists of compromised values, should not impose composition rules and should not force periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Many organizations still enforce complexity, expiration and minimum age, and the exam may refer to them. Password best practices cover length, complexity, reuse, expiration, age (how long a password must be kept before it can be changed), compromised credential monitoring, account auditing and a policy report that shows compliance.

Attribute-based access control: decisions using attributes.
Privileged access management: secures admin access.

out: Name the four OAuth roles and what each one does.
Follow the Authorization Code flow with PKCE step by step.
Explain access tokens, refresh tokens, scopes, expiry and revocation.
Decide when OIDC, Authorization Code, Client Credentials or the Device flow fits.
plain: Imagine lending a parking valet a key that starts the car but cannot open the boot, and that stops working at midnight. You never hand over your own key. OAuth works like that: an app receives a limited, expiring pass instead of your password. OpenID Connect adds a signed note saying who you are.
tech: OAuth 2.0 defines four roles. The resource owner is usually the user. The client is the application that wants access. The authorization server authenticates the user, records consent and issues tokens. The resource server is the API holding the data, and it accepts or rejects tokens. Scopes name what the client may do, such as reading a calendar, and the granted scopes can be narrower than those requested.

In the Authorization Code flow the client sends the browser to the authorization server. The user signs in and approves the request. The browser returns to a pre-registered redirect URI with a short-lived, single-use code. The client then exchanges that code at the token endpoint, over a back channel, for tokens. Exact matching of the redirect URI stops an attacker from sending the code somewhere else.

Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) protects that code. The client creates a random code verifier, sends a SHA-256 hash of it as the code challenge at the start, and reveals the verifier only when exchanging the code. An attacker who steals the code cannot produce the verifier. The current OAuth security best practice, RFC 9700, requires protection against code injection and recommends PKCE for all clients, including ones with a secret. It also says the Implicit grant should not be used and the Resource Owner Password Credentials grant must not be used.

An access token is presented to the resource server and should be short-lived and narrowly scoped. A refresh token lets the client get a new access token without asking the user again, is sent only to the authorization server, and should be rotated or sender-constrained for public clients. Expiry is automatic. Revocation ends access early, as RFC 7009 describes. A self-contained JSON Web Token (JWT) access token can often keep working until it expires, even after revocation, unless the resource server checks with the authorization server. That is one reason lifetimes are kept short.

The Client Credentials grant is for one service talking to another with no user present. The Device Authorization grant suits input-limited devices such as televisions. OpenID Connect adds authentication on top of OAuth: requesting the openid scope returns an ID token, a signed JWT intended for the client, that states who authenticated. An ID token should not be sent to APIs, and an access token should not be treated as proof of who signed in.
terms: The party who can grant access, usually the user.
The service that authenticates users and issues tokens.
The API that holds the data and checks tokens.
A named limit on what a token permits.
The registered address the authorization server sends the browser back to.
A short-lived, single-use value exchanged for tokens.
Proof Key for Code Exchange: proves that the client exchanging a code is the one that requested it.
A credential presented to an API.
A longer-lived credential used only to obtain new access tokens.
A signed JWT from OpenID Connect stating who authenticated.
JSON Web Token: a compact signed set of claims.
Ending a token's validity before it expires.
An OAuth grant in which a service acts as itself.
eg: A project tool asks to read a user's calendar. The consent page lists calendar read only, and the tool never sees the user's password.
An administrator revokes a reporting integration. New refresh attempts fail at once, and any JWT access token already issued stops working when it expires unless the API checks revocation.

walks.title: Follow Authorization Code with PKCE
steps: The client creates a random code verifier and hashes it to make a code challenge.
The client redirects the browser to the authorization server with its client ID, redirect URI, scopes, state value and code challenge.
The user signs in and approves the scopes.
The authorization server redirects back to the registered URI with a single-use code.
The client checks the state value, then posts the code and the original verifier to the token endpoint.
The authorization server hashes the verifier, compares it with the challenge and issues tokens.
The client calls the resource server with the access token.

labs.title: Compute a PKCE challenge and read a JWT, offline
labs.tool: openssl and base64 in your lab VM, using no real tokens
do: In your VM, set the published test verifier from RFC 7636 Appendix B: V=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk
Run: printf %s "$V" | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | base64 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '='
Compare the output with the RFC's expected challenge, E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM
Make a harmless token payload: printf '{"sub":"lab-user","scope":"calendar.read","exp":1893456000}' | base64 and then decode it again with base64 -d. Note that anyone can read an encoded payload.
Write one sentence on why encoding is not encryption. Use only sample values, and never paste a real token into any tool.
labs.expect: Your computed challenge matches the RFC value exactly, and the decoded payload shows the sample claims.
labs.explain: PKCE works because a hash cannot be reversed to reveal the verifier. JWT payloads are signed, usually not encrypted, so they must not hold secrets.
pass: Your challenge matches the published value.
You can explain why a stolen code alone is useless when PKCE is used.

qs.s: In OAuth 2.0, which component accepts or rejects access tokens when an API is called?

a.w: It hosts the API and checks each token presented.
It issues tokens, but the API call goes elsewhere.
It presents tokens and does not judge them.
The owner grants consent and does not check tokens.

qs.s: What does PKCE specifically protect against?

a.t: Use of a stolen authorization code
a.w: The thief cannot supply the original code verifier.
PKCE does not change password strength.

a.t: A user approving too many scopes
a.w: Consent design and policy handle this.

qs.s: Where should a client send a refresh token?

a.w: It is exchanged there for new access tokens.
This exposes a powerful credential widely.

a.t: To the resource owner's browser storage for sharing
To the identity of the next client
a.w: Tokens are not passed between clients.

qs.s: An administrator revokes an integration, but its self-contained JWT access token still works for ten more minutes. What explains this?

a.t: The API validates the JWT locally until it expires
a.w: Local validation does not consult revocation state.

a.t: Revocation always requires a server restart
a.w: Restarting is not part of revocation.

a.t: The refresh token has become an ID token
OAuth does not support revocation at all

qs.s: Match each situation to the best OAuth choice.
pairs: A nightly job calls an API as itself
A mobile app acts for a signed-in user
A television shows a code to enter on a phone
qs.why: Ask who is acting, and whether that party can use a browser and hold a secret.

qs.s: True or false: an ID token should be sent to an API as proof of access.

a.w: An ID token is intended for the client and describes authentication.

mistakes: Treating a successful OAuth grant as proof of who the user is. Use OIDC for sign-in.
Assuming revocation stops every token instantly.
Asking for broad scopes up front because it is easier than asking later.
sum: OAuth delegates limited, expiring access without sharing passwords.
Authorization Code with PKCE is the normal choice when a user is present.
Access tokens go to APIs, refresh tokens go to the authorization server, and ID tokens go to the client.
cards: What does PKCE prove?
That the client exchanging a code is the one that started the request.
Which OAuth token goes only to the authorization server?
The refresh token.
What adds an ID token on top of OAuth?
OpenID Connect.
lessons.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect in depth
lessons.why: Almost every modern product connects to other products. OAuth decides how much access those connections receive and how that access ends, so misunderstanding it leads to over-granted, long-lived access that nobody can see.
lessons.scenario: A single-page app needs to read a user's documents through an API on that user's behalf. A developer suggests collecting the user's password and sending it to the API. What should be used instead?
lessons.answer: The Authorization Code flow with PKCE and a narrow read scope. The app never handles the password, access is limited and expiring, and the user or an administrator can revoke it. The password grant must not be used.

product: The consent screen is where a person grants another product access to their work, often without reading it. Scope names written for developers, such as files.readwrite.all, mean little to the person approving them. The experience also continues long after consent: tokens expire, integrations break, and administrators need a way to see and end access.

eng: Which scopes do we support, and can they be split further?
How quickly does revocation take effect, given our token lifetimes?
prod: What happens to the customer's workflow when an integration disconnects?

ex.title: Design a third-party integration and consent experience
ex.scenario: You are designing a B2B SaaS application. A customer wants to connect its workspace to an external analytics platform that requests access to projects and user activity.
ex.problem: The current flow shows a raw list of scopes and an Allow button. Once connected, integrations are invisible, and nobody knows what they can reach.
tasks: Design the connection flow from starting in your product through consent and back.
Write the permission and consent screen, with plain-language scope explanations.
Design token expiration and reconnection states.
Design the integrations list, including what each one can access and last used.
Design revocation, including what happens to the integration's data.
constraints: Authorization Code with PKCE is the expected flow, and the product never sees the other service's password.
Requested scopes should be the minimum needed, and the granted scopes may be narrower.
Revocation may not stop existing access tokens until they expire.
needs: Users need to understand what they are granting.
Workspace administrators need to approve, review and revoke integrations.
Integration builders need to know why they were refused a scope.
ex.deliver: A connection flow, consent screen, reconnection states and an integrations management screen.

crit.t: The design reflects the real OAuth flow, including expiry, refresh and revocation.
Excessive scopes, a malicious consent request and an offboarded installer are addressed.
A person can say in plain words what the integration will be able to do.
The design covers the full life of an integration, including who owns it when its installer leaves.

seniors: Ask what happens when the person who connected an integration leaves the company, since its access may depend on their account.
Be accurate about revocation timing, because "access removed immediately" may not be true.

cq.s: An analytics app needs to read project names, yet it asks for full read and write on all workspace data. What should the product support?

a.t: Clear scopes, with admins able to refuse excess requests
a.w: Visibility and admin control encourage least privilege before access is granted.

a.t: Approving automatically if the app comes from a known company
a.w: A familiar name doesn't justify write access that it doesn't need.

a.t: Hiding detailed scopes so that the consent screen looks simpler
a.w: Simplicity that hides the grant defeats the purpose of consent.

a.t: Granting everything now and asking the vendor to reduce it later
a.w: Access has already been over-granted by the time anyone asks.
